Aśvaghopa
Bud.; son of Suvarṇākṣī; pupil of Pārśva or of Pārśva's pupil Puṇyayaśas; contemporary of Kaniṣka (or 2nd Cent. A. D.); taken, not on much evidence, a. the founder of Mahāyāna; wrongly identified by some with Āryaśūra an. Mātṛceṭa. For a Tibetan tradition identitying him with Kālidāsa see J. of the G. Jha. Res. Inst. I. iv. (1944) p.. 403 ff. [Page435-a.
For Aśvaghoṣa-Kālidāsa parallels etc. see NCC. IV. p. 63b. There seem to have been more than one Aśvaghoṣa an. many works ascribed to him are apocryphal.
For a study on his works, see S. Levi, J.. 213 (July-Dec. 1928) p.. 193-216; J. Nobel, Nachrichten der Gesselschaft der Wissenschaften in Gottingen, 1931, p.. 380-336.
On him, see Ency. Rel. & Eth. II. p. 159; J.. 1892. Vol. XIX. p. 201 ff. 1908. Vol. XII. p. 57 ff; Ind. Ant. 1903. p.. 345-360; B. C. Law, Aśvaghoṣa, RASB. Monograph Ser. 1946.
Kvs. intro. p.. 25-29; two verses ascribed to him in the Sbhv. are found in Bhartṛhari's Nītiśataka.
On his identity with Dhārmika Subhūti cited by Vasubandhu (Abhi. Kośa III. 59) an. a. of Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānakārikā an. Pañcagatidīpana, see S. Levi, J.. 414 (July-Dec. 1928). p.. 204-7.
According to Vasubandhu, he is supposed to have assisted Kātyāyanīputra in his C. on the Abhidharma.
For a traditional life-account of Aśvaghoṣa, see Nanjio 1460.
See also It-Sing p.. 165. 181, for reference to some poetical songs of his an. the Sūtrālaṅkāra, besides the Buddhacarita.
On his use of epic Sanskrit see Sukumar Sen, JASB. XXVI. (1930). p.. 181-206.
On figures of speech in his works, see H. R. Diwakar: Les fleurs de rhetorique dens l'Ind., Etudes sur le developpement des “alaṅkāra” on [Page435-b] ornaments stylistiques la litterature Sanskrite, Paris, 1930, ch. V. p.. 55-71.
